text: The most straightforward exfiltration pattern is exactly what a baseline deviation is built to catch: an unusually large outbound transfer to a destination the host has no history with, often at a time it isn't normally active. Flow data is well-suited to spotting this across an entire network, because volume, destination, and timing are exactly the fields a flow record carries.

Almost every firewall allows outbound DNS by default, because normal internet use depends on it. DNS tunneling abuses exactly that trust — encoding stolen data into the subdomain portion of DNS queries and sending a steady stream of them to an attacker-controlled domain, which decodes the data and can even smuggle commands back in its responses. It looks like ordinary port 53 traffic until you notice abnormally long query names and an unusual volume aimed at one obscure domain.

Beaconing is malware phoning home to a command-and-control server at a fixed, regular interval to check in for instructions, whether or not data is moving at that exact moment. The destination alone often isn't suspicious — the rhythm is. No ordinary browsing or working produces connections spaced with that kind of mechanical regularity, and it only shows up as a pattern across many flows reviewed over time, not in any single flow record.

A realistic case stacks these signals: flow data shows a destination outside the host's baseline, recurring every 60 seconds like clockwork, to a domain registered only a few weeks ago — and a DPI pull on that host shows an abnormal volume of unusually long DNS queries going to that same domain. No single signal proves anything alone, but a baseline deviation, a beaconing interval, a new domain, and confirmed DNS tunneling together make a strong case.

That layered reasoning — flow data for breadth, baselining for context, DPI for confirmation — is exactly how this chapter's tools work together against a real threat. Next up, Chapter 4 moves from the network to the endpoint itself: EDR telemetry, what actually gets collected on a host, and why.
